study.title: Study of Judas 1
study.overview: Judas writes as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James to people called, sanctified by God the Father and guarded by Jesus Christ. He begins by desiring mercy, peace and love, but soon explains why he writes: there are people infiltrated into the community that distort the grace of God, deny the Lord and threaten the faith of the saints. To warn the church, Judas resort to known examples of the Scriptures: Israel in the desert, rebellious angels, Sodom and Gomorrah, and also figures such as Cain, Balaam, and Korah. In contrast to the false teachers, believers are called to remember the words of the apostles, build up in faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and treat the vacillating with discernment and mercy. The chapter ends with a doxology that concentrates security and hope on God's ability to keep his own and present them blameless with joy.

outline.title: Greeting and motive of the letter
outline.explanation: Judas presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, addresses the so-called, sanctified and guarded, and explains that the letter was written to exhort to battle for the faith of O to the saints, because some ungodly infiltrated and perverted the grace of God.

outline.title: Warning through examples of judgment
outline.explanation: The author recalls the judgment on unbelieving Israel, upon the angels who have abandoned their position and on Sodom and Gomorrah, and applies these examples to deceivers who determinate the flesh, reject sovereignty, and speak arrogantly about what they do not understand.

outline.title: Portrait of false masters and called to persevere
outline.explanation: Judas describes these men as following the way of Cain, the deception of Balaam and the rebellion of Korah; denounces his attitudes in assemblies, his spiritual sterility and his lack of the Spirit, and then recalls the words foretold by the apostles on scourging in recent times.

outline.title: Final Exhortations and Praise to God
outline.explanation: The loved ones must build up in the most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in the love of God and expect the mercy of Christ. They must also exercise mercy with discernment, save some with fear and trust in him who is powerful to keep them without stumbling and presenting them joyful before divine glory.

study.context: The letter shows a Christian community already exposed to false teachers. The text itself uses language of dispute, apostolic remembrance, and examples of the Old Testament to respond to a doctrinal and moral crisis. The notes provided highlight that Judas writes to establish believers in the received Christian faith and in the conduct consistent with it, especially in the face of opposition by seduction and corruption.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that common salvation does not authorize spiritual relaxation; it calls a persevering struggle for apostolic faith. The grace of God is not permission for immorality, but the scenario in which holiness must be preserved. Jude also insists on the reality of God's judgment on unbelief, rebellion, and ungodliness, showing that sin is not only a private fault, but an affront to divine sovereignty. At the same time, the text preserves a strong emphasis on perseverance: believers are guarded by Jesus Christ, must remain in God's love and can rely on divine power to sustain them to the end. The pastoral response includes firmness against error and prudent mercy toward people in different degrees of spiritual danger.

scholarViews.insight: The note about Judas 1:5 understands that the deliverer of Israel in the exodus is the pre-incarnate Jesus himself, and uses this judgment on the unbelievers as a direct warning against false teachers.

The note about Judas 1:3 states that the purpose of the letter is to establish believers in the Christian faith and in a practice consistent with it, especially when there is opposition by seduction or persecution.
The note over Judas 1:25 highlights that all glory, majesty, dominion, and power belong to the one wise God our Saviour in all ages, and not to men who exalt themselves.

questions: What signs of the text show that Judas sees false doctrine as a moral, not just intellectual danger?
How does the memory of the examples of judgment in the past help the church discern the present without falling into excessive fear or hardness?
How can we unite firmness in truth and practical mercy in dealing with spiritually vulnerable people?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to vigilance and perseverance. Examine whether you are just knowing the faith or really battling for it with obedience, prayer, and discernment. Strengthen your prayer routine in the Holy Spirit, keep in communion with the church and avoid messages or influences that turn grace into a leave to sin. At the same time, do not treat people in error with automatic contempt: help with fear, truth and compassion, always trusting that God is the one who keeps his own.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are brief excerpts and, in some cases, treat other books or have very summarized formulations; so I used only what was explicitly present and applicable to the chapter. The biblical text here was taken as the main one, but the numbering and some expressions appear in the form of paraphrase, not as standard canonical translation.
